Q: Why does `default( None )` not always appear to produce `None` A:
  • foo | default(None) evaluates to null
  • {{ foo | default(None) }} evaluates to an empty string ""
Note: All Jinja expressions closed in double braces {{ expression }} evaluate to strings.

Given

  bar: "{{ foo | default(None) }}"

the task

  - debug:
      msg: bar is empty string
    when: bar | length == 0

gives

  msg: bar is empty string

But the task

  - debug:
      msg: foo is empty string
    when: foo | default(None) | length == 0

fails with the error:

"... object of type 'NoneType' has no len() ... "

As a result in ternary, an empty string selects FALSE and null selects NONE.

Notes:

  1. See the Note in Omitting Parameters

  2. Both null and empty string "" select FALSE in ternary if the third parameter is omitted. The tasks

  - debug:
      msg: "{{ bar | ternary('TRUE', 'FALSE') }}"
  - debug:
      msg: "{{ foo | default(None) | ternary('TRUE', 'FALSE') }}"

give

  msg: FALSE
  msg: FALSE

Q: Is it possible to run fio with libaio on Android to measure raw UFS performance, and if not, what is the recommended approach? A:

A long time ago fio used to be shipped as part of the AOSP (build?) environment but it's since been ripped out and even back then it wasn't built with the libaio ioengine. Taking a stab at your questions:

  1. It's definitely possible to statically link fio (see https://github.com/axboe/fio/blob/fio-3.41/configure#L223 ) but it's on you to build a copy of libaio that would run in an Android environment. I think the bigger question is whether Android's kernel is built with CONFIG_AIO because if it's not then that's an insurmountable roadblock to going with this.
  2. If you stick with fio but can't do 1. I/O submission options open to are not so low overhead but yes you can use the psync ioengine (just be aware using the iodepth option doesn't make sense with a synchronous ioengine). The posixaio ioengine may also not be usable/available depending on Android's bionic libc. Due to its nature using direct I/O means that you are robbing the kernel of creating parallelism for you with a non-async ioenigne so you will have to rely on options like numjobs to build up multiple in-flight I/Os.

Q: Why does Float'Succ behave differently on Float-variables than on Float-expressions? A:

I posted this as a bug (https://gcc.gnu.org/bugzilla/show_bug.cgi?id=124163), but it was rejected. The observed behavior is claimed to be justified because the differences are between static and dynamic operations.

Ada.Numerics.Pi is a named number so every static operation is performed with infinite precision on it, include 'Succ and 'Adjacent.

I have understood this to some extent now, will update the conclusion in the question.

some way to display it:

to inspire you,

    // menu user

Q: npm ERR! husky - .git can't be found WINDOWS A:

In my case, everything was fine except parent folder of the project had .git.

Husky found a problem as .git in parent folder whereas project in child folder of it.

I removed .git from parent folder as git was mistakenly init in parent folder.

Q: "How to pass absolutely no value where it is passing omit_place_holder ?"

A1: Some filters also work with omit as expected. For example, the play

- hosts: localhost
  vars:
    test:
      - "{{ var1|default(false) }}"
      - "{{ var1|default(omit) }}"
  tasks:
    - debug:
        msg: "{{ {'a': item}|combine({'b': true}) }}"
      loop: "{{ test }}"

gives

  msg:
    a: false
    b: true

  msg:
    b: true

As a sidenote, default(omit) is defined type string

    - debug:
        msg: "{{ item is defined }}"
      loop: "{{ test }}"
    - debug:
        msg: "{{ item|type_debug }}"
      loop: "{{ test }}"

give

TASK [debug] *************************************************************
ok: [localhost] => (item=False) => 
  msg: true
ok: [localhost] => (item=__omit_place_holder__6e56f2f992faa6e262507cb77410946ea57dc7ef) => 
  msg: true

TASK [debug] *************************************************************
ok: [localhost] => (item=False) => 
  msg: bool
ok: [localhost] => (item=__omit_place_holder__6e56f2f992faa6e262507cb77410946ea57dc7ef) => 
  msg: str

A2: No value in Ansible is YAML null. Quoting:

This is typically converted into any native null-like value (e.g., undef in Perl, None in Python).

(Given my_int_L4=bob). If the variable my_int_http defaults to null instead of omit

profiles:
      - "{{ my_int_L4 }}"
      - "{{ my_int_http | default(null) }}"

the list profiles will be undefined

  profiles: VARIABLE IS NOT DEFINED!

Use None instead

profiles:
      - "{{ my_int_L4 }}"
      - "{{ my_int_http | default(None) }}"

The variable my_int_http will default to an empty string

  profiles:
  - bob
  - ''

See also section "YAML tags and Python types" in PyYAML Documentation.

Q: usefullness of shared_ptr in C interface A:

Perhaps the make_shared is a specialized one that places the shared pointer into some global container before returning to the caller.

It seems odd that the only operations on an opaque wrapper object would be to create and destroy it, so there must be missing code that is relevant to the question.

You stated:

I don't understand the purpose of this. The client code obviously cannot enforce shared_ptr semantics, so the only ref counting is done in C++ side.

I agree with your second sentence. The conclusion is that there should be interface code that accepts your wrapper object as a parameter and is then manipulated by C++ code.
